transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-19
Start time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Sanjay Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Liu (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Morales (ArborCare Head of AI), Greg Turner (Infra Lead), Priya Sharma (Security), Tom Blake (Procurement)

Summary:
ArborCare is a regulated med-device org evaluating a private, walled-site deployment of Redwood to support clinical transcription and triage models. Main concerns: offline update/update-signing process, hardware constraints (no H100 allowed yet, limited rack space, A100 gen2 preferred), patching windows, auditing (SOC2/ISO-style evidence), data egress restrictions, and fallback to hosted in emergencies. Team wants concrete runbook for air-gapped install, verification steps, and a pricing comparison vs Dedicated.

Topics covered:
- Network isolation and allowed jumpbox patterns
- Firmware & model update signing + transport (sneakernet vs signed package via jumpbox)
- Hardware footprint and GPU support matrix (A100 vs H100 vs L40)
- Operational runbooks for weekly/quarterly patches
- Telemetry and audit logs without egress
- Rollback & canary strategies in hermetic environments

Transcript:
[00:00] Sanjay (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for carving out the time today, we really appreciate you walking us through the constraints, want to make sure we cover the install story, hw, update cadence and what's required for audits.
[00:18] Dr. Elena Morales (ArborCare): thanks, yeah short context — ArborCare runs a clinical triage service and by regulation our inference endpoints must run in a walled facility, no outbound internet. we've done pilots on hosted but can't keep PHI outside our network. so the question is can Redwood run fully offline, and how do updates and proofs-of-origin work.
[00:40] Maya (Redwood SE): absolutely — we've done these with a few medtechs. there are two typical patterns: fully airgapped with signed artifact import via a jumpbox that has tightly controlled egress, or a sealed-transfer (sneakernet) where packages are physically transported on a signed USB and validated by an HSM or KMS in your network. both approaches have tradeoffs.
[01:05] Greg (Infra): we prefer not to introduce a device that ever sees the public net. so the sneakernet option is appealing. but our operations team is allergic to manual steps every week; we need an automated verification step and checksum signing we can audit.
[01:26] Priya (Security): and from security we need evidence of code provenance and a tamper-proof log. we cannot rely on plain sha checksums sitting in an email. we use an on-prem HSM for signing keys. what does that look like with Redwood?
[01:42] Maya: good question. our recommended pattern: Redwood produces a signed release bundle, we also provide a detached signature that your HSM can verify against our public key. alternately, you can do a trust-on-first-use: import our public key into your HSM then verify every bundle on ingress. if you want an extra layer, we can also provide an intermediate signing step: you sign a manifest with your HSM after we provide the artifact, that manifest is stored locally and used during install.
[02:12] Tom (Procurement): cost-wise, how much overhead does the sealed-install process add? we need a rough delta vs hosted API and vs Redwood Dedicated.
[02:25] Sanjay: good callout. sealed-install engineering + packaging is a one-time onboarding professional service — we usually quote a fixed integration fee (ranges we've seen: $30k–$75k depending on complexity) plus ongoing support and a private deployment license. Dedicated is in-between: you still need network controls but less packaging work because we manage some connectivity. i'll follow up with a tailored number.
[02:52] Dr. Elena: hardware — we currently have racks with two A100 80GB cards per node, can't get H100s this fiscal. our rack space is tight: max 6U per inference cluster. can Redwood run on our A100 setup and what perf compromises are we looking at?
[03:14] Maya: yes A100s are supported. practical notes: model selection and quantization matter. with A100 80GB you can run larger models but might need bfloat or int8 profiles to hit latency targets. our runtime supports continuous batching and can tune batch sizes to balance latency vs throughput. i can attach a perf profile we ran for a similar footprint — note those numbers are noisy because of sequence length differences.
[03:40] Greg: we also run an older kernel on our OS for certified drivers; we are limited to CUDA 11.5 variants. will that break anything?
[03:52] Maya: we try to support a matrix — but some of our newer optimizations assume newer CUDA. if you're on 11.5 we will validate the runtime and may need a tiny shim or to pin a compatible build. that is part of the one-time integration work.
[04:10] Sanjay: what about telemetry? if the cluster cannot phone home, can we still get logs and metrics for you to support SLA calls?
[04:20] Priya: yep we need an auditable trail. but all logs must stay on-prem. we can provide read-only access through a jumpbox or provide a scheduled export on encrypted media.
[04:35] Maya: we have two models here: push telemetry to your internal observability stack (Prometheus, ELK) over private network, or collect locally and generate signed, time-stamped bundles for support cases. for urgent incidents you can opt-in to a temporary, customer-initiated outbound session (jumpbox tunnel) so our support can triage — that session is tied to an access window and logged by your SSA system.
[05:00] Greg: who holds keys for the model weights? are they encrypted at rest and in transit in the sealed workflow?
[05:08] Maya: yes at-rest encryption is standard. for sealed installs, we recommend your HSM hold the decrypt key and we ship encrypted blobs. the node's runtime can request the key from the HSM via an internal KMS connector. this avoids storing plain weights on disk prior to install.
[05:30] Dr. Elena: any special firmware/BIOS requirements? our procurement has firmware whitelists and we need to show compatibility.
[05:38] Maya: we produce a hardware compatibility doc with minimum BIOS settings, driver versions, and recommended kernel flags. for air-gapped installs we'll include a firmware checklist. if you need signed firmware images we can work with your vendor — that's often customer-driven.
[05:54] Tom: on the support side, how fast can Redwood respond for an outage? do we need a hot-swap fallback model?
[06:02] Sanjay: SLAs vary by plan. for private installs we normally offer an enterprise support contract with a next-business-day hardware replacement for on-prem parts but we also offer options for 24/7 coverage and an on-call rotation for critical incidents. for model-level failures we can offer a lightweight fallback: a small, lower-capacity local model that runs even during degraded states; remote help is limited by your policy though.
[06:26] Priya: audit readiness — we will need reproducible evidence of updates, who approved them, and a signed chain of custody for any deployed artifact. do you provide an audit ledger style export?
[06:40] Maya: yes we can generate a signed install record for each deploy that includes artifact hash, signature, installer id, HSM verification result, and user approval metadata. we also keep an internal release log we can export on demand to you as a signed tarball.
[06:58] Dr. Elena: can you explain rollback mechanics — if a model update causes regressions how do we revert in a sealed environment?
[07:07] Maya: retain previous bundles locally; our runtime supports atomic swaps and keep-last-n versions. in hermetic mode you simply pick the prior signed bundle ID and restore; the runtime validates signatures again before activation. we also support staged rollouts across nodes if you want a canary.
[07:28] Sanjay: i'll add that we can recommend a canary ratio — 10% of nodes for 24–48 hours then expand. in walled sites with small clusters, the canary is often a single node.
[07:42] Greg: okay capacity planning — our throughput target is 120 reqs/sec at p95 latency under 600ms for a 512-token model. what's the ballpark for a three-node A100 cluster?
[07:56] Maya: off the cuff, a 3x A100 80GB cluster with batching tuned could be in range but depends on sequence length distribution and KV cache hit rate. i'll mark this for a perf bench: we can run a representative trace you provide and return a tested QPS/latency profile.
[08:16] Dr. Elena: that bench would be critical for our board and procurement. can Redwood run the bench in your hosted infra to model latency, or do you need the exact on-prem hw?
[08:28] Maya: for initial sizing we can run in-hosted with similar GPU types and scale down accounting for kernel/CUDA differences. for high confidence we prefer an on-site bench with your images; we can also ship a bench container you run and send us the raw trace.
[08:46] Tom: procurement will need licensing terms: is there a per-token meter in private installs or a seat-based model?
[08:55] Sanjay: private deployments are typically license + support. we provide either usage reporting for internal chargebacks or a capacity-based fee. we can map it to a token-equivalent for comparison with hosted. i'll include both models in the quote.
[09:08] Priya: data retention — if a clinician deletes a record upstream, how does Redwood ensure we don't keep derived embeddings or caches?
[09:17] Maya: we support TTLs and retention policies. in private mode we adhere to your retention policy and can run a purge job that removes kv cache entries and regenerates caches. we also offer a verification step to prove purge completion.
[09:33] Greg: update windows — our maintenance policy is weekly windows on Sundays 02:00–05:00 local. can Redwood batch updates into that window?
[09:42] Maya: yes — updates can be scheduled only during your maintenance windows. the runbook includes a dry-run verification, checksum validation and a staged restart strategy to keep at least N-1 nodes active where possible.
[09:57] Dr. Elena: one more thing: our compliance team requires signed attestations for people who approve deploys. can Redwood integrate with our SSO and require an approver token before install?
[10:09] Maya: we integrate with SAML/OIDC. the install manifest can include an approver SSO token and we record the user identity in the signed install record.
[10:20] (brief cross talk)
[10:40] Sanjay: okay sounds like next practical milestone is: Maya shares the sealed-install runbook + hw checklist; we schedule a perf bench; and i produce a pricing comparison. any other must-haves?
[10:53] Dr. Elena: please include a sample signed install artifact and a walkthrough of the HSM verification. our auditor will want to see the chain.
[11:02] Maya: will do, i'll include an example manifest, a verification script, and a sample signed tarball (with fake keys) so you can test your HSM flow.
[11:12] Tom: on contracting: we'll want liability language around PHI exposure in the SLA and an escalation path. are you able to show precedent language?
[11:22] Sanjay: yes we'll share a redlineable SOW and example enterprise agreement. we'll mark PHI-specific liability and define a joint incident response MOU.
[11:32] Greg: curious: have you dealt with magnetic tape transfer for long-term archives? some of our sites still use LTO.
[11:39] Maya: yes — we've shipped archive bundles via LTO in a few groovy older hospitals. awkward but doable; we recommend signed manifests and checksum lists on a separate medium.
[11:52] Dr. Elena: any third-party components in the runtime that would complicate our supply chain review?
[11:59] Maya: runtime includes open-source libs and some vendor-optimized kernels. we can provide SBOMs and we track CVEs and remediation timelines. the integration packaging will include material to satisfy your supply chain team.
[12:15] Sanjay: good question, we'll also include a list of any third-party kernel blobs and licensing notes.
[12:24] Priya: about emergency fallbacks — if there is a catastrophic failure, can you ship a 'hot' package we can apply offline to recover service fast?
[12:34] Maya: yes we can pre-stage a validated recovery bundle that you keep physically on-site, signed and ready. the runtime supports rapid bootstrap from that bundle.
[12:44] Dr. Elena: timeframe — if we decide to proceed, how long from PO to go-live?
[12:49] Sanjay: typically 8–12 weeks for a sealed private deployment: 2–3 weeks for onboarding and legal, 3–6 weeks for integration and validation, 1–2 weeks for benching and rollout. that varies with site readiness.
[13:03] Greg: ok we'll need a detailed project plan.
[13:06] Sanjay: we'll send an outline.
[13:12] (silence, note-taking)
[13:30] Maya: small note on runtime tuning — KV cache eviction policies can drastically change memory needs. if your workload has high prefix overlap we can achieve big wins on latency and reduce token compute. otherwise expect higher memory consumption.
[13:51] Dr. Elena: is there any way to run a part of the stack in dedicated hosted and part on-site to reduce hardware needs? hybrid?
[13:59] Maya: yes hybrid routing is possible but with data residency constraints you likely can't send PHI. we can run non-PHI components hosted — e.g., model evaluation or anonymized telemetry — while inference stays on-site. we support policy-based routing that routes by tag.
[14:19] Tom: one more: training/fine-tuning — will Redwood support secure model updates if we want to fine-tune periodically with local data?
[14:28] Maya: we don't provide training as a managed service in private installs yet, but we can support model patching workflows where you produce fine-tuned weights and we help validate and package them. some customers run internal fine-tune pipelines and send signed artifacts to us for packaging.
[14:45] Dr. Elena: procurement timeline — we aim for board signoff in mid-August. will that fit your sales cadence?
[14:53] Sanjay: yes that aligns well. we'll target follow-ups in the next two weeks and the on-site validator in early August.
[15:02] (wrap up)
[15:15] Sanjay: recap: Maya deliver runbook + sample artifacts by 7/23; Sanjay deliver quote by 7/22; schedule perf bench and on-site validator — i'll coordinate with Greg. any other items?
[15:29] Dr. Elena: no that's it. thanks everyone.
[15:34] (meeting closed)
